# Citation integrity

Build a claim-to-source ledger before formatting references. Retrieve each record
from an authoritative index or the publisher, preserve DOI, PMID, PMCID, title,
authors, venue, year, version, and retrieval time, and record whether full text,

Write `citation-ledger.csv`, `references.bib`, and `citation-audit.md`. The audit

1: # The REporting of A Disproportionality Analysis for DrUg Safety Signal Detection Using Individual Case Safety Reports in PharmacoVigilance (READUS-PV): Explanation and Elaboration
2: 
3: - PMCID: PMC11116264
4: - DOI: 10.1007/s40264-024-01423-7
5: - Primary source: https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC11116264
6: - Retrieved: 2026-07-18T03:59:56.758118Z
7: 
8: ## Abstract
9: 
10: Abstract In pharmacovigilance, disproportionality analyses based on individual case safety reports are widely used to detect safety signals. Unfortunately, publishing disproportionality analyses lacks specific guidelines, often leading to incomplete and ambiguous reporting, and carries the risk of incorrect conclusions when data are not placed in the correct context. The REporting of A Disproportionality analysis for drUg Safety signal detection using individual case safety reports in PharmacoVigilance (READUS-PV) statement was developed to address this issue by promoting transparent and comprehensive reporting of disproportionality studies. While the statement paper explains in greater detail the procedure followed to develop these guidelines, with this explanation paper we present the 14 items retained for READUS-PV guidelines, together with an in-depth explanation of their rationale and bullet points to illustrate their practical implementation. Our primary objective is to foster the adoption of the READUS-PV guidelines among authors, editors, peer reviewers, and readers of disproportionality analyses. Enhancing transparency, completeness, and accuracy of reporting, as well as proper interpretation of their results, READUS-PV guidelines will ultimately facilitate evidence-based decision making in pharmacovigilance. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s40264-024-01423-7.
11: 
12: ## Key Points
13: 
14: **table-wrap.** READUS-PV guidelines comprise 14 items for reporting disproportionality studies. Their uptake will help enhance transparency, completeness, and accuracy, facilitating evidence-based decision making.
15: 
16: ## Background
17: 
18: Individual case safety report (ICSR) databases collect reports of suspected adverse drug reactions (ADRs) from both healthcare professionals and patients [ 1 ]. Disproportionality analyses, exploring ICSR databases to identify unexpected associations (in terms of nature or clinical presentation) between drugs and adverse events, when combined with a clinical review of the cases, provide valuable insight into emerging drug safety concerns, notably for ADRs that are unlikely to be fully captured by clinical trials [ 2 – 7 ]. Their apparent simplicity has led to a surge in the quantity of published disproportionality analyses [ 8 ], rising from 40 in 2017 to 180 in 2021 according to PubMed data [ 9 ] (presumably an underestimate because of the lack of standardization in reporting). This surge potentially overwhelms decision makers and contributes to these results being disregarded due to the high ratio of noise to signal. Additionally, it may also directly influence patients and clinical practice [ 10 ]. Notwithstanding, almost 75% of the published studies present some type of spin , or distortion of study findings, which in disproportionality analysis may manifest as inadequate reporting, overstatement in the interpretation of the findings, or causal statements without taking into account underlying biases that may be sufficient to explain the association [ 11 , 12 ]. This lack of proper reporting and interpretation in research is concerning, as it impedes the utilization and comprehension of research findings and contributes to research waste [ 13 – 15 ].
19: 
20: To address this issue, in an international effort, we developed the READUS-PV guidelines ( RE porting of A D isproportionality analysis for dr U g S afety signal detection using ICSRs in P harmaco V igilance) [ 16 ]. Comprising 14 reporting recommendations (plus four for the abstract), these guidelines aim to (1) assist authors in the preparation of transparent, complete, and accurate articles; (2) allow self-assessment and replicability; (3) promote an adequate understanding of the results and their limitations; and (4) assist reviewers and editors in the evaluation of disproportionality analysis for publication.
21: 
22: READUS-PV is published as a set of two papers. In the development and statement paper, we outline the steps taken to build the checklist [ 17 ]. In this explanation and elaboration paper, aligning with the structure of EQUATOR Network guidelines [ 18 ] and using streamlined terminology (see Box 1 for a glossary of terms used), we substantiate the inclusion of each item and provide bullet points detailing each recommendation. Additional sub-items were also proposed, which provide supplementary information that may enhance the completeness and usability of the study.
23: 
24: **Box 1.** Glossary of terms
25: 
26: ## READUS-PV Recommendations
27: 
28: ### Title
29: 
30: Item 1. Title Information
31: 
32: The title should comprehensively but succinctly convey the study’s focus, using clear language, and avoiding ambiguity and striking titles that could generate unjustified alarm or safety endorsement [ 20 ].
33: 
34: Item 1a If disproportionality analyses are a prominent component of the published study, the study should be identified as a ‘disproportionality analysis’. The type of data and name of the database(s) should be specified .
35: 
36: Explanation: Including ‘disproportionality analysis’ in the title facilitates identification by potential users, appropriate indexing in databases and screening for knowledge synthesis. This helps to provide a specific context for the analysis and informs the reader about the nature of the data under investigation. While alternative terms (e.g., ‘case/non-case analysis’) have also been used, consistent use of ‘disproportionality analysis’ going forward will reduce ambiguity and simplify the extraction for future meta-research and systematic reviews. Non-specific terms are not recommended because they do not optimally align to the study design and could result in misunderstandings.
37: 
38: Essential elements:
39: 
40: - The study should be identified as a ‘disproportionality analysis’ in the title.
41: - Avoid non-specific (e.g., ‘data mining’, ‘real-world’, ‘pharmacovigilance’, ‘cross-sectional’, or ‘retrospective study’) and misleading (e.g., increased risk) terms.
42: - Identify the type of data in the title, specifying ‘ICSRs’ or other terms if appropriate (e.g., ‘social media’).
43: - Clearly mention the name/acronym of the database(s) used (e.g., ‘FDA Adverse Event Reporting System’, ‘Eudravigilance’, ‘VigiBase’) in the title.
44: 
45: Additional elements:
46: 
47: - Any other important quantitative analysis used in conjunction should be specified (e.g., ‘pharmacovigilance/pharmacodynamic analysis’ or ‘a disproportionality analysis and systematic review’).
48: - When the study design is broader (e.g., hybrid design combining different data sources such as systematic review with meta-analysis and a disproportionality analysis) or the use of ‘disproportionality analysis’ in the title may be reductive, include the term at least among the keywords.
49: 
50: Item 1b. Report the name of adverse event(s) and/or drug(s) under study, when applicable .
51: 
52: Explanation: The title should inform about the object(s) of the study. For example, a disproportionality analysis could explore (1) a specific drug-event combination (DEC); (2) the overall safety profile of a drug or its safety in a subgroup of users (e.g., looking at differences between sexes, or age groups); (3) the spectrum of potential iatrogenic determinants of a disease; and (4) methodological developments.
53: 
54: Essential elements:
55: 
56: - Identify the research topic in the title, including the drug(s) and/or event(s) investigated.
57: 
58: Additional elements:
59: 
60: - Consider mentioning the population investigated, for example when the analysis has been restricted to a specific therapeutic indication or to reports concerning pregnancy or children.
61: 
62: ### Introduction
63: 
64: Item 2. Background
65: 
66: In reporting a disproportionality analysis, it is crucial to provide the reader with a clear explanation of the scientific background and rationale for the study. This section sets the foundation for understanding the subsequent objectives, methods, and results, and helps the reader appreciate the significance and relevance of the study.
67: 
68: Item 2a. Describe the drug(s) and its utilization, the nature of the adverse event(s) under study and its frequency, and the existing knowledge on the drug-event combination.
69: 
70: Explanation: The investigation of any research question should be preceded by the collection of evidence already accrued. The specific gap in knowledge should be identified based on limitations of previous studies, conflicting results, or unanswered needs.
71: 
72: Essential elements:
73: 
74: - When a specific drug(s) is under study, describe their relevant features, including the active ingredient (preferably using the international nonproprietary name), therapeutic class, mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, indications, and target populations, as applicable.
75: - When a specific adverse event(s) is under study, describe their relevant features, providing details about its nature, clinical manifestations, severity, seriousness, and impact on the patient’s quality of life.
76: - Describe the research question under study, present evidence supporting it, and discuss known risk factors: previously identified pertinent signals (e.g., when investigating liver failure, present previous signals of increased transaminases for the same drug), and information retrieved from regulatory documents (e.g., Summary of Product Characteristics).
77: - Highlight the specific gap in knowledge that necessitates further investigation, explaining why the current understanding is insufficient.
78: 
79: Additional elements:
80: 
81: - Consider including further information on the drug(s), including brand names, formulations, administration routes, posology, dosing regimens, and duration of use.
82: - Consider including information about the expected number of patients exposed, the average duration of exposure, and the background rate of the event(s), as they impact the number of ICSRs [ 21 , 22 ].
83: - Consider including information about the approval date and any relevant warning [ 23 , 24 ].
84: 
85: Item 2b. Specify the rationale for performing the analysis, e.g., as part of routine pharmacovigilance, to investigate an overall safety profile, or to assess a prespecified hypothesis.
86: 
87: Explanation: By specifying the rationale, the reader gains a clear understanding of the purpose and context of the analysis. Conception of a disproportionality analysis, excluding methodological studies, can usually be summarized as follows [ 25 – 27 ]: (1) reporting of signals emerging from agnostic/untargeted pharmacovigilance activities (e.g., emerging from routine analyses on the entire ICSR database without a prespecified hypothesis); (2) investigation of the overall safety profile of a specific drug (e.g., in case of conditional accelerated approval or a specific risk management plan [ 28 ]); (3) assessment of a prespecified evidence-based hypothesis (e.g., based on pharmacological plausibility, recent case report/series, or imbalances observed in clinical trials).
88: 
89: Essential elements:
90: 
91: - Explain the rationale for performing the disproportionality analysis (see explanation).
92: 
93: Item 2c. Explain why ICSR databases and disproportionality analysis are suitable to fill the knowledge gap.
94: 
95: Explanation: Regardless of the journal type, authors should carefully address the nature of spontaneous reporting data and the appropriateness of using disproportionality analysis to investigate the research question [ 29 ]. Notably, as with any study, the availability of already published pharmacoepidemiological and/or ICSR studies should be carefully considered before planning a disproportionality analysis, to avoid research waste and redundancies [ 25 ]. In particular, the question arises on the actual added value of a newer but similar analysis using the same ICSR database or datasets generating overlapping signals of disproportionate reporting (SDRs) [e.g., WHO VigiBase vs. US FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS)] [ 30 ]. Replication studies should be carefully justified as efforts to offer an additional novel complementary perspective, for instance by providing a case-by-case analysis or by accounting for previously unrecognized biases to assess the validity of a signal.
96: 
97: Essential elements:
98: 
99: - Justify the ability of disproportionality analysis to fill the knowledge gap. If other studies addressing the same (or in good part similar) question are available, explain the actual added value of the current disproportionality analysis (e.g., a bias that has been previously neglected, new target population, different dosing regimen, new indication, accelerated approval, rare events, methodological limitations of previous studies).
100: 
101: Additional elements:
102: 
103: - Consider concisely explaining, and providing appropriate reference for, the nature of ICSRs and disproportionality analyses.
104: - In scientific journals not specialized in pharmacology and pharmacovigilance, consider more exhaustively explaining the nature of ICSRs and disproportionality analyses.
105: 
106: Item 3. Objectives
107: 
108: The aims should directly align with the research question(s) and provide specific objectives.
109: 
110: Item 3. State specific objectives, identifying the adverse event(s), the drug(s), and the reference group, including any prespecified hypothesis, if applicable.
111: 
112: Explanation: An explicit and concise statement of the objective(s) will help readers understand the goal and assess whether the data and methods used adequately address it. Such statements may be written in the form of objectives or questions, including the event(s) and drug(s) under investigation, and the reference group used for comparison. Question formulation frameworks such as PICO (population, intervention, comparator, outcome) or PEO (population, exposure, outcome) could also help in formulating the objective(s) [ 31 , 32 ], in the lack of frameworks specific to disproportionality.
113: 
114: Essential elements:
115: 
116: - Provide an explicit and concise statement of all primary and secondary objective(s) or question(s), logically progressing from the knowledge gap.
117: - Clearly define the adverse event(s) and drug(s) under investigation.
118: 
119: Additional elements:
120: 
121: - Specify when the disproportionality analysis has not been implemented to investigate reactions (drug-event association) but rather the co-occurrence of reactions (event-event association) [ 33 ], the influence of indication on ADRs (drug-indication-event association), or drug interactions (drug-drug-event associations) [ 34 ].
122: 
123: ### Methods
124: 
125: Item 4. Study design
126: 
127: Presenting key elements of the study design early in the paper allows readers to quickly grasp the context and framework of the study, ensuring greater comprehension.
128: 
129: Item 4a. Identify the study (i.e., ‘disproportionality analysis’) and the type of data used (e.g., ‘individual case safety reports’).
130: 
131: Explanation: As already explained for the title, the use of standardized terminology should be preferred to simplify study appraisal and reduce ambiguity.
132: 
133: Essential elements:
134: 
135: - Identify the study as a ‘disproportionality analysis’.
136: - Specify the type of data used (e.g., ICSRs).
137: 
138: Item 4b. Provide an outline of the entire study design, including primary and sensitivity analyses performed, and other designs such as case-by-case analysis or literature review.
139: 
140: Explanation: The study design should be presented in a clear and structured manner, with appropriate justification for each operational choice, to facilitate critical assessment, replication, and interpretation of the study.
141: 
142: Essential elements:
143: 
144: - Introduce the primary analysis with a clear reference to the study objectives.
145: - Introduce sensitivity/secondary analyses as efforts to address potential sources of bias or uncertainty in the study, to check analysis assumptions, or to investigate effect modifiers or specific populations.
146: - Specify whether a case-by-case causality assessment and/or a systematic review of the literature were conducted.
147: 
148: Additional elements:
149: 
150: - For more complex study designs, consider including a flow diagram providing a clear overview of the design elements, such as data sources, population selection, exposure assessment, and stratifications.
151: - In case a more complex study design is implemented, consider consulting other published checklists for the reporting (cfr. Table 3 in the Statement article).
152: 
153: Item 5. Data description, access, and preprocessing
154: 
155: Provide a well-referenced description of the database(s), including its extent and relevance to the research question.
156: 
157: Item 5a. Specify the name of the database(s), the database(s) custodian, and the coverage. Specify the type/number of drugs included within the database and the thesaurus, taxonomies, or ontologies used for coding drugs and events.
158: 
159: Explanation: Information about the database content allows a correct interpretation of the results since disproportionality analysis is intrinsically based on comparing the ICSRs of interest with the underlying database. Given that reporting rate, drug utilization, and background rate may differ across countries, and due to masking bias (see later), the content of the database strongly affects the results.
160: 
161: Essential elements:
162: 
163: - Specify the name of the database(s) used in the analysis.
164: - Identify the database custodian [i.e., entity responsible for managing the databases)].

167: - Identify the thesaurus, taxonomy, or ontologies used for coding drugs and events and the version. 168: - Specify the size of the database (number of reports).

173: - Consider providing information on data collection (e.g., possibility of a selection bias) and anonymization.
174: - Consider describing quality measures applied to ensure integrity and reliability of data.

177:

201: Item 6b. Describe the nature and the meaning of key variables assessed in the work.
202: 
203: Explanation: Ensure that readers have a clear understanding of the key variables being assessed and how they relate to the research question, to simplify appraising the appropriateness of the analyses and of the interpretation of the results. For example, it is important to clarify which criteria were used to determine seriousness (e.g., death, hospitalization, life-threatening, disability).
204: 
205: Essential elements:
206: 
207: - Describe the nature and meaning of key variables, such as whether they are continuous (e.g., age), binary (e.g., seriousness), or categorical (e.g., reporter qualification, or country).
208: - Describe the management of key variables with missing values (e.g., sex unspecified).
209: 
210: Item 6c. Specify and justify any grouping of drugs or events. For drugs, specify and justify whether active ingredients/trade names/salts were considered and/or the selected role.
211: 
212: Explanation: Ensure clarity in defining the objects of the study. The choices should be justified based on factors such as clinical relevance, data availability, pharmacological interactions, or specific research objectives [ 44 , 45 ].
213: 
214: When grouping multiple drugs or events, the authors should refer to existing taxonomies (e.g., MedDRA or ATC [ 35 , 36 ]), standardized MedDRA queries (SMQs), previous studies, knowledge engineering techniques, and justified and detailed expert opinions, or, alternatively, provide a clear clinical rationale [ 43 , 46 , 47 ].
215: 
216: Essential elements:
217: 
218: - Specify and justify the assigned roles of drugs (suspect primary and secondary/concomitant/interacting).
219: - Specify and justify the focus on active ingredients, trade names, or specific salts.
220: - Specify and justify any groupings of drugs and/or adverse events, for primary, secondary and/or sensitivity analyses.
221: 
222: Additional elements:
223: 
224: - Consider providing the list of free text mapped to the drug of interest.
225: 
226: Item 6d. Describe any additional data source used, the type of data, and how they interact with ICSRs.
227: 
228: Explanation: The refinement, validation, and prioritization of safety signals generated from disproportionality analysis often requires evidence from other data sources and methods [ 14 ]. Clinical trial reports, literature reviews, regulatory documents, and datasets of labeled ADRs may help assess expectedness [ 48 ]. Pharmacodynamic/pharmacokinetic, bioinformatic, and chemoinformatic data help explore pharmacological plausibility [ 49 ]. Healthcare and claims databases (other sources of real-world data) point to a possible alternative explanation and public health and clinical impact [ 50 ].
229: 
230: Essential elements:
231: 
232: - Describe any additional data source and the type of data.
233: - Describe how these data were linked to ICSRs and SDRs.
234: 
235: Item 7. Statistical methods
236: 
237: Describe all statistical methods, including those used to control confounding, selective reporting, and other biases specific to disproportionality analyses, and provide rationale.
238: 
239: Item 7a. Present any descriptive analysis performed, specifying variables investigated, statistical tests, and significance thresholds.
240: 
241: Explanation: Descriptive analysis can help to identify patterns and trends in the data and help identify and characterize both expected and unexpected confounders and effect modifiers. Geographical characterization helps exploring the impact of different pharmacovigilance systems, local warnings, and populational specificities.
242: 
243: Essential elements:
244: 
245: - Present any descriptive analysis performed.
246: 
247: Additional elements:
248: 
249: - Specify and justify any reference/comparator group.
250: 
251: Item 7b. Describe the measure(s) selected for the disproportionality analysis, including any threshold used to identify SDRs. Explain the reason for this choice if applicable.
252: 
253: Explanation: Although the choices of disproportionality measures, thresholds and algorithms for identifying SDRs have shown to impact their performances to detect known ADRs [ 6 , 43 , 51 , 52 ], they are poorly reported in published articles [ 11 ]. Common measures used in 2D disproportionality analyses include the reporting odds ratio (ROR) [ 53 ], proportional reporting ratio (PRR) [ 54 ], information component (IC) [ 55 ], and the Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean [ 6 , 51 , 56 , 57 ]. Measures used for investigating interactions (i.e. 3D) include Ω and INTSS (interaction signal score) [ 58 , 59 ].
254: 
255: Essential elements:
256: 
257: - State the disproportionality measure used, including its dimensionality (e.g., 2D or 3D).
258: - Specify whether units are ICSRs or drug-event pairs (more than one per ICSR).
259: - Specify and justify the comparator group (e.g., non-cases) [ 60 ].
260: - Specify any ICSR and statistical threshold adopted for identifying an SDR.
261: - Explain methods used for investigating drug interactions or other risk factors, if applicable.
262: 
263: Additional elements:
264: 
265: - Consider explaining the disproportionality measure using a contingency table.
266: 
267: Item 7c. Clearly describe any sensitivity analysis and any tool to control confounding, including any restriction, subgroup, stratification, adjustment, or interaction.
268: 
269: Explanation: Sensitivity/secondary analyses aim to explore the robustness of the results to various assumptions and methodological choices made, and to control for confounding or effect modifiers, to the extent possible with ICSRs [ 3 , 61 ].
270: 
271: An extensive description of the list of biases in the analysis of ICSR databases is beyond the scope of this guideline, and the reader should refer to previous reviews on this topic [ 1 , 3 , 62 , 63 ].
272: 
273: Essential elements:
274: 
275: - Describe and justify any sensitivity analysis.
276: 
277: Item 7d. Specify the variables and methods used for the case-by-case analysis, including any algorithm or criteria used to assess causality, if performed.
278: 
279: Explanation: The synthesis of ICSR characteristics and the assessment of the causal role of drugs at the case-level [ 64 – 67 ] is a crucial task in validation and prioritization of SDRs and need to be described, taking into account dechallenge/rechallenge, concomitant drugs, time to onset, and, whenever available, medical history/comorbidities, narratives [ 64 – 67 ].
280: 
281: Essential elements:
282: 
283: - Provide a clear description of the variables analyzed in the case-by-case analysis.
284: - Describe any method used for causality assessment.
285: 
286: Item 7e. Specify any statistical methods used for other data sources.
287: 
288: Explanation: Because there is little evidence about approximation of risk estimates by disproportionality analyses [ 68 , 69 ], any correlation with external data should be acknowledged as a merely theoretical investigation, for example, to explore pharmacological drug mechanisms [ 70 , 71 ].
289: 
290: Essential elements:
291: 
292: - Specify any statistical methods used for other data sources.
293: 
294: ### Results
295: 
296: Item 8. Description of reports
297: 
298: Describe in detail the ICSR selection process (i.e., the number of reports included and excluded at each step).
299: 
300: Item 8a. Specify the number of ICSRs included at each stage, including reasons for exclusion.
301: 
302: Explanation: Authors should report the number of ICSRs included at each stage of the study to simplify tracking and evaluate the sample size.
303: 
304: Essential elements:
305: 
306: - Report the number of ICSRs and cases included at each stage of the study.
307: - Report the reasons for exclusions (e.g., duplicates, incomplete ICSRs, exclusion criteria).
308: 
309: Additional elements:
310: 
311: - Consider using a flow diagram [ 72 ].
312: 
313: Item 8b. Provide key demographic and clinical characteristics of cases, comparing cases with any appropriate reference group if possible.
314: 
315: Explanation: This item can help provide a better understanding of the population being studied and any potential confounders or susceptibility factors, such as age, sex, comorbidities, or concomitant drugs [ 42 ]. The appropriate reference group will depend on the specific research question and study design (e.g., the entire ICSR database vs. other reports recording the same medication).
316: 
317: Essential elements:
318: 
319: - Present the results of the descriptive analysis.
320: 
321: Additional elements:
322: 
323: - Consider presenting this information in a table.
324: 
325: Item 9. Results of disproportionality analyses
326: 
327: Describe in detail the results of disproportionality analyses.
328: 
329: Item 9. Present all results, including confidence intervals, as well as results of sensitivity analyses, if performed.
330: 
331: Explanation: The reporting of all disproportionality results allows the readers to independently derive their interpretation from the results of the study. Providing, even in supplementary material, the figures of the contingency tables and the number of expected ICSRs may help readers to better understand the data underlying the calculations.
332: 
333: Essential elements:
334: 
335: - Clearly present the results of the analysis, including point estimates, confidence intervals, and results of any sensitivity analyses. Provide the figures of the contingency tables.
336: - Provide the number of expected ICSRs.
337: 
338: Item 10. Results of case-by-case analysis
339: 
340: Describe in detail the results of the case-by-case analysis, including the variables investigated.
341: 
342: Item 10. Present the case-by-case analysis of key variables, as well as the causality assessment, if applicable.
343: 
344: Explanation: The analysis of cases included in the calculation of disproportionality estimates may help readers and decision makers to evaluate the validity of the results. These variables include the drug’s suspected role, concomitants, alternative causes, underlying disease, time to onset, the outcome after dechallenge and/or rechallenge, dose and route, sex, age, and other events. The results emerging from the causality assessment should also be included in the presentation. The case-by-case analysis should provide a detailed synthesis of all, or a subset of, ICSRs prioritized using criteria or algorithms [ 73 ], which can help in identifying specific factors contributing to adverse events and assessing causality. Remember that an anonymization may be necessary to minimize the risk of re-identification of patients notably in rare diseases and/or drugs.
345: 
346: Essential elements:
347: 
348: - Present the results of key features from the case-by-case analysis, quantifying missing values.
349: - Present the results of the case-level causality assessment.
350: 
351: Additional elements:
352: 
353: - Consider providing a list of ICSRs with all the variables assessed, in the form of a table.
354: 
355: ### Discussion
356: 
357: Item 11. Key results
358: 
359: It is wise to begin the discussion with a short summary of the key results with reference to study objectives. This section will help readers assess whether the subsequent interpretation and implications offered by the authors are supported by the findings.
360: 
361: Item 11. Discuss key results with reference to study objectives, and contextualize them within the current literature and other consulted sources. Clearly discriminate between expected reactions and emerging safety signals.
362: 
363: Explanation: By carefully discussing the characteristics of the ICSRs, key results, contextual evidence, and pharmacological plausibility, the authors can provide valuable insights into the validity of the safety signal(s) and the safety profile of the drug(s). All stakeholders should consider that the prevalent perspective in pharmacovigilance is that an SDR alone cannot prove causation and does not allow to calculate incidence or compare risks between drugs [ 12 , 25 , 74 , 75 ]. Similarly, interpretation of a lack of statistically significant disproportionality (negative finding) as an absence of risk or of an inverse disproportionality signal (i.e., a lower-than-expected reporting) as a protective drug-related effect is discouraged [ 76 ]. In performing the aggregated causality assessment integrating existing and new evidence, the authors are referred to the Bradford Hill guidelines [ 77 – 80 ].
364: 
365: Essential elements:
366: 
367: - Present key results distinguishing between expected reactions and emerging safety signals as applicable.
368: - Contextualize results with existing knowledge, highlighting inconsistencies and new findings.
369: - Contextualize results with pertinent information on the regulatory landscape, recent changes in prescribing patterns, and warnings.
370: - Discuss pharmacological plausibility, considering mechanism of action, pharmacokinetics, and other relevant factors.
371: - Negative results must also be presented and discussed, in the light of positive/negative control events for contextualization (e.g., establish basic assay sensitivity/specificity).
372: 
373: Item 12. External validity
374: 
375: Discuss the external validity of the study results.
376: 
377: Item 12a. Discuss the external validity of the results to the general population.
378: 
379: Explanation: External validity refers to how well the results of a study can be generalized to other populations and settings. ICSR databases, compared with clinical trials, are likely to be more representative of real-world scenarios, accounting for factors such as comorbidities, misuse, and comedications. However, if cases analyzed share a peculiar characteristic, for example overdose or misuse, the safety concerns identified may not be relevant to clinical settings.
380: 
381: Essential elements:
382: 
383: - Discuss the generalizability of results, with reference to setting, catchment area, disease prevalence, drug utilization, population characteristics, unusual patterns of reporting (e.g., litigation-related or solicited reports).
384: 
385: Additional elements:
386: 
387: - If applicable, consider discussing how different access to medication, diagnostic procedures, warnings, and regulatory actions may have resulted in different reporting rates among countries, and how they may have biased the results [ 81 , 82 ].
388: 
389: Item 12b. Discuss the potential relevance of results in clinical practice.
390: 
391: Explanation: The proposed risk minimization measures should not only be based on the results and limitations of disproportionality analyses but also the validity of the safety signal(s) considering all sources of evidence. These proposals may include updates to drug labels, additional monitoring requirements, or restrictions on use in certain patient populations. It is important to carefully consider the potential benefits and risks. Providing recommendations based on disproportionality alone should be avoided.
392: 
393: Essential elements:
394: 
395: - Propose relevant and balanced clinical/regulatory risk minimization strategies, if applicable.
396: 
397: Item 12c. Propose further study designs, if applicable.
398: 
399: Explanation: If the study identified a safety signal, propose further studies to refine, support, or refute the signal, quantify the risk, and identify risk factors. Healthcare databases are traditionally viewed as a complementary source of postmarketing real-world evidence and are suited for hypothesis testing.

405: Item 13. Limitations
406: 
407: Present general limitations of ICSR databases and specific limitations of the strategy implemented.
408: 
409: Item 13. Present general limitations, making it clear that disproportionality analyses alone cannot prove causation or measure incidence, and specific limitations, including confounding and reporting bias and efforts to mitigate them.
410: 
411: Explanation: It is crucial to discuss the limitations of the study to provide a balanced and appropriate interpretation of the findings. If multiple data sources were used, the limitations of each source and method should be discussed.
412: 
413: Disproportionality analysis alone can be one step towards identifying safety signals but cannot formally prove causation or measure incidence due to lack of details about patient exposure [ 3 , 74 ], reporting biases [ 3 , 82 ], and confounding biases. Efforts should be made to control for these factors through appropriate statistical methods or study design and to consider them as alternative explanations for the findings.
414: 
415: Finally, the adequacy of the database(s) and the information captured on key variables should be discussed in relation to the study objectives, including factors such as completeness, accuracy of coding, and consistency of reporting.
416: 
417: Essential elements:
418: 
419: - Present general limitations of ICSR databases and disproportionality analyses.
420: - Present specific limitations and efforts implemented to mitigate them.

422: ### Declarations
423: 
424: Item 14. Declarations
425: 
426: Provide clear and exhaustive declarations about data and software used, data and code availability, and conflicts of interest.
427: 
428: Item 14a. Provide the source of funding/sponsorship and the role of the funders/sponsors for the present study and for any original study on which the present article is based.
429: 
430: Explanation: This item helps readers assess the likelihood of potential conflicts of interest. It should also be disclosed whether the funder or sponsor has been involved in defining the question, collecting, and analyzing data, interpreting results, or approving the final report.
431: 
432: Essential elements:
433: 
434: - Disclose sources of financial (e.g., salary) or non-financial (e.g., analytical service, access to commercial dataset) support, specifying relevant grant ID numbers for each funder. If no specific financial or non-financial support was received, this should be declared.
435: - Explicitly report any interests (commercial, financial, or intellectual) that the funder/sponsor/author(s) may have in obtaining certain results.
436: - Disclose any active involvement of the funder/sponsor (e.g., defining the question, collecting and analyzing the data, interpreting the results, or approving the final report). If funders or sponsors had no role in the study, this should be declared.
437: 
438: Item 14b. Clearly identify potential commercial and intellectual conflicts of interest (e.g., link to any drug/event investigated, whether financial, legal action, or software used).
439: 
440: Explanation: It is essential for authors to transparently disclose any potential commercial or intellectual conflicts of interest that might have influenced the study design, results, discussions, or conclusions. For instance, authors may have links to the drug or event under investigation, received financial compensation from companies involved in the study or related to its topic, or been engaged in legal actions involving the company or product being researched, or a competing product. Additionally, if authors used software or other tools developed or owned by a specific company, this could also influence the study’s results and discussions.
441: 
442: Essential elements:
443: 
444: - Disclose any of the authors’ relationships or activities that readers could consider pertinent or that could have influenced the study.
445: - If any authors had competing interests, report how they were managed.
446: 
447: Item 14c. Declare any institutional approval needed or granted in the investigation.
448: 
449: Explanation: Examples of such approvals may involve Ethics Committee or Institutional Review Boards (IRB), regulatory agencies, or data access committees. The manuscript should state the name of the approving body and the reference number or other identifying information.
450: 
451: Essential elements:
452: 
453: - Declare any institutional approval.
454: 
455: Item 14d. Include a statement on data availability, code availability (including the version of the statistical software used), and protocol registration.
456: 
457: Explanation: By sharing data, analytic codes, and other materials, others can reuse the data, identify potential errors, attempt to replicate the findings, and gain a deeper understanding of the analysis beyond what is described in the Methods section [ 83 ]. Several publicly accessible repositories, such as Open Science Framework, Dryad, and Figshare, are available for hosting shared materials, and provide a URL/DOI. The clean dataset(s) used for analysis may be shared in a readily reusable format, such as a CSV file. For code sharing, authors can provide the analytic code used in software with a command-line interface or detailed step-by-step descriptions for point-and-click software. Additionally, it is essential to mention the software used, along with its version number, in the Methods section, or a separate statement about the statistical analysis methods. If authors encounter barriers preventing them from sharing certain materials due to legal or licensing restrictions (e.g., commercial databases), they should make a clear declaration about it.
458: 
459: Essential elements:
460: 
461: - Declare whether preprocessing data, postprocessing data, and code are available. Provide a URL or DOI.
462: - Provide the URL or DOI to the protocol, if applicable.
463: - Specify the software used and its version.
464: 
465: ### Abstract
466: 
467: Explanation: An abstract providing key information about the main objective(s), methods, results, and implications of the findings should help readers decide whether to access the full report. For some readers, the abstract may be all that they have access to. Therefore, results must be presented for all main outcomes for the main objective(s) regardless of the statistical significance, magnitude, or direction of effect. Terms presented in the abstract will be used to index the disproportionality analysis in bibliographic databases. Therefore, reporting keywords that accurately describe the question (such as population, drug, and event) is recommended. Of note, meta-epidemiological studies and several articles have highlighted the common misinterpretation (also called spin) of results from disproportionality analyses in published studies, notably in abstracts. Indeed, many disproportionality analyses intentionally or unintentionally overstate the strength of causal links, lack proper handling and discussion of biases, or over-extrapolate results to provide clinical recommendations, comparing drug safety profiles or claiming that a drug is well tolerated [ 12 , 20 , 25 , 74 , 75 , 84 ]. We therefore encourage authors to appropriately present and interpret their findings in abstracts, which are often the only part of articles read and accessible to everyone.

474: 
475: This explanation and elaboration paper justifies and details the selected reporting recommendations for disproportionality analysis. The adoption and editorial support of READUS-PV guidelines will have a positive impact on the reporting of disproportionality analyses conducted using ICSR databases. Increased transparency and accuracy resulting from improved reporting will benefit the research community, leading to enhanced evidence-based decision making and better patient care.

# The REporting of A Disproportionality Analysis for DrUg Safety Signal Detection Using Individual Case Safety Reports in PharmacoVigilance (READUS-PV): Explanation and Elaboration

## Structured Scientific Account

- **Authors**: Fusaroli M, Salvo F, Begaud B, AlShammari TM, Bate A, Battini V, Brueckner A, Candore G, Carnovale C, Crisafulli S, Cutroneo PM, Dolladille C, Drici MD, Faillie JL, Goldman A, Hauben M, Herdeiro MT, Mahaux O, Manlik K, Montastruc F, Noguchi Y, Norén GN, Noseda R, Onakpoya IJ, Pariente A, Poluzzi E, Salem M, Sartori D, Trinh NTH, Tuccori M, van Hunsel F, van Puijenbroek E, Raschi E, Khouri C
- **Source**: *Drug Safety*, 2024 June
- **DOI**: [10.1007/s40264-024-01423-7](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40264-024-01423-7)
- **PMCID**: [PMC11116264](https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC11116264)
- **PMID**: [38713347](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38713347/)
- **Companion Statement Paper**: DOI [10.1007/s40264-024-01421-9](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40264-024-01421-9)
- **Protocol**: [https://readus-statement.org/](https://readus-statement.org/)
- **Reference Count**: 84
- **Retrieved from Europe PMC**: 2026-07-18

---

## Abstract

Disproportionality analyses of individual case safety report (ICSR) databases are a cornerstone of pharmacovigilance signal detection, yet their reporting has been hampered by inconsistency, incompleteness, and frequent interpretive distortion. In response, the international READUS-PV collaboration developed a set of 14 reporting recommendations across all manuscript sections (title through declarations), plus four additional items for abstracts. This explanation and elaboration paper provides the detailed justification for each retained item, alongside bullet-pointed implementation guidance. The guidelines are organized to span the title, introduction (background and objectives), methods (study design, database description, variable definitions, and statistical methods), results (report selection, disproportionality estimates, and case-by-case synthesis), discussion (key results, external validity, and limitations), and declarations (funding, conflicts of interest, institutional approvals, and data/code availability). Adoption of READUS-PV is intended to improve transparency, completeness, and accuracy in the reporting of disproportionality analyses and thereby support evidence-based pharmacovigilance decision making.

---

## Introduction

ICSR databases aggregate suspected adverse drug reaction reports from healthcare professionals and patients. Disproportionality analyses mine these databases to identify associations between drugs and adverse events that deviate from background reporting patterns; when combined with clinical review, they can reveal emerging safety concerns—particularly those unlikely to surface in premarketing clinical trials [2–7].

However, the volume of published disproportionality analyses has grown sharply. PubMed-indexed studies in this category climbed from approximately 40 in 2017 to roughly 180 in 2021 [9], a figure likely underestimated because of unsystematic terminology in reporting [8]. This increase risks overwhelming decision makers with noise and may also directly influence patients and clinical practice [10]. Critically, a meta-epidemiological investigation found that nearly 75% of published disproportionality analyses exhibit spin—inadequate reporting, overstated causal claims, or omission of biases that could explain observed associations [11,12]. Such distortions impede utilization and contribute to research waste [13–15].

To address these deficits, an international team developed the READUS-PV guidelines—the REporting of A Disproportionality analysis for drUg Safety signal detection using individual case safety reports in PharmacoVigilance [16]. The 14-item core checklist (plus four abstract items) was designed to assist authors in preparing transparent and reproducible articles, enable self-assessment and replication, promote proper interpretation of findings with their limitations, and aid reviewers and editors in evaluating submissions.

The READUS-PV output is published as two papers: a development and statement paper that describes the consensus process [17], and the present explanation and elaboration paper that substantiates each retained item with rationale and practical bullet points. The structure follows the EQUATOR Network model for reporting guideline documents [18].

---

## Methods (Guideline Development Summary)

The present paper is an explanation and elaboration document; the full development methodology is reported in the companion statement paper (DOI 10.1007/s40264-024-01421-9) [17]. In brief, the authors constituted an international panel of pharmacovigilance experts who followed a consensus-based approach to identify, refine, and select the final set of reporting recommendations. The protocol was preregistered on the EQUATOR registry and made available at [https://readus-statement.org/](https://readus-statement.org/).

The current explanation paper organizes the 14 retained items into the following domains: title; introduction (background and objectives); methods (study design, data description and preprocessing, variable definitions, and statistical methods); results (description of reports, disproportionality results, and case-by-case analysis results); discussion (key results, external validity, and limitations); and declarations. Each item is presented with (a) an explanation of the rationale for its inclusion and (b) essential bullet points that operationalize the recommendation. Additional sub-items are proposed where supplementary detail may enhance completeness or usability.

The companion paper's Table 3 also cross-references other published checklists for situations where the study design extends beyond a pure disproportionality analysis.

The study received a certification from the Research Ethics Committee of the University Hospital of Bordeaux that formal ethics submission was not required under French regulation. Funding was provided by Alma Mater Studiorum – Università di Bologna via the CRUI-CARE open-access agreement. Several co-authors disclosed employment relationships with pharmaceutical companies (Bayer AG, GSK, Pfizer) and declared stock ownership; the remaining authors declared no competing interests related to this work.

---

## Results: The 14 READUS-PV Reporting Items

### Item 1 — Title Information

**Item 1a**: The study should be identified as a "disproportionality analysis" in the title, and the type of data and database name should be specified.

Including the term "disproportionality analysis" facilitates database indexing, retrieval for systematic reviews, and appropriate reader context-setting. Non-specific labels (e.g., "data mining," "real-world study," "cross-sectional study," or "retrospective study") are discouraged because they obscure the study design and risk misinterpretation. The title should also name the data source (e.g., "ICSRs," or "social media" if applicable) and the specific database (e.g., FDA Adverse Event Reporting System [FAERS], EudraVigilance, VigiBase).

Additional recommendations: when other quantitative methods are used concurrently (e.g., a pharmacovigilance-pharmacodynamic analysis, a systematic review), this should be noted in the title. For hybrid designs where "disproportionality analysis" alone would be reductive, the term should appear at minimum among the keywords.

**Item 1b**: Report the name of adverse event(s) and/or drug(s) under study, when applicable.

The title should communicate the substantive focus—whether a specific drug-event combination, the overall safety profile of a drug (or a subgroup such as pediatric or pregnant populations), the iatrogenic determinants of a disease, or a methodological advancement.

### Item 2 — Background

**Item 2a**: Describe the drug(s) and their utilization, the nature and frequency of the adverse event(s), and the existing knowledge on the drug-event combination.

The introduction should summarize relevant drug features (international nonproprietary name, therapeutic class, mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, indications, and target populations) and adverse-event features (nature, clinical manifestations, severity, seriousness, and impact on quality of life). The specific knowledge gap should be justified by reference to prior evidence—previous disproportionality signals (e.g., elevated transaminases when liver failure is the focus), regulatory documents such as Summaries of Product Characteristics, and limitations of existing studies.

Additional information that may be considered includes brand names, formulations, administration routes, posology, dosing regimens, expected patient exposure, average duration of exposure, and background event rates, as these affect the number of reports received [21,22]. Approval dates and regulatory warnings may also be relevant [23,24].

**Item 2b**: Specify the rationale for performing the analysis—e.g., part of routine pharmacovigilance, investigation of an overall safety profile, or assessment of a prespecified hypothesis.

Disproportionality analyses typically originate from three contexts [25–27]: (1) agnostic or untargeted routine pharmacovigilance activities without a prespecified hypothesis; (2) investigation of the overall safety profile of a specific drug (e.g., under conditional accelerated approval or a risk management plan [28]); or (3) assessment of a prespecified evidence-based hypothesis grounded in pharmacological plausibility, recent case reports or series, or imbalances observed in clinical trials.

**Item 2c**: Explain why ICSR databases and disproportionality analysis are suitable for addressing the knowledge gap.

Authors should justify the appropriateness of spontaneous reporting data for the research question [29]. In particular, publication of a new disproportionality analysis should be preceded by careful consideration of existing pharmacoepidemiological or ICSR-based studies to avoid redundancy [25]. When substantial overlap exists with earlier work—for example, signals of disproportionate reporting (SDRs) from VigiBase versus FAERS [30]—replication studies must explicitly articulate their incremental contribution, such as a novel case-by-case analysis or adjustment for previously unrecognized biases.

### Item 3 — Objectives

State specific objectives, identifying the adverse event(s), the drug(s), the reference group, and any prespecified hypothesis.

An explicit and concise statement of aims—potentially framed using the PICO (population, intervention, comparator, outcome) or PEO (population, exposure, outcome) format [31,32]—should logically follow from the knowledge gap. Both primary and secondary objectives should be listed. Authors should also clarify when the analysis investigates relationships beyond simple drug-event associations, such as event-event co-occurrence [33], drug-indication-event relationships, or drug-drug interactions [34].

### Item 4 — Study Design

**Item 4a**: Identify the study as a "disproportionality analysis" and specify the data type (e.g., ICSRs).

Consistent terminology reduces ambiguity and aids appraisal. Standardized designation should be carried from title to methods.

**Item 4b**: Provide an outline of the entire study design, including primary and sensitivity analyses, and other components such as case-by-case analysis or literature review.

The design should be presented in a structured manner with justification for each operational choice. The primary analysis should be introduced with explicit reference to study objectives. Sensitivity and secondary analyses should be framed as efforts to address confounding, check assumptions, or investigate effect modifiers or subgroups. The presence or absence of a case-by-case causality assessment and/or systematic literature review should be stated.

For complex hybrid designs, a flow diagram is recommended. Authors may also consult the checklist cross-references provided in the companion statement paper (Table 3).

### Item 5 — Data Description, Access, and Preprocessing

**Item 5a**: Specify the database name, custodian, coverage, number of drugs, and the thesauri or ontologies used for coding drugs and events.

Database content directly determines the denominator of disproportionality calculations and influences results through reporting rates, drug utilization patterns, background event rates, and masking bias. The report should identify: the database(s) by name; the custodian entity; temporal and geographical coverage; the types of medicinal products captured (or the number and class of drugs, for industry databases); the coding systems—commonly the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) for events and Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classification for drugs [35,36]—including the version used; and the total number of reports in the database.

Additional considerations include justification for database choice, information on data collection and potential selection bias, and any quality-assurance measures applied.

**Item 5b**: Specify extraction dates and describe and justify all data-preprocessing choices, including transformations and exclusions.

Preprocessing decisions can alter the results and their interpretation [37,38]. Authors should report: the extraction or download date and access mechanism (e.g., online portal, data-sharing agreement, dashboard, quarterly data release) with a URL if available; any required approvals; restrictions on data access; procedures for identifying and removing duplicates, handling missing or nullified data, managing incongruous or inconsistent values, dealing with follow-up information, and standardizing data elements (e.g., free-text drug names to active ingredients); any derived variables (e.g., dose, time-to-onset, comorbidity proxies) and the assumptions underlying them; and any data exclusions applied.

### Item 6 — Variable Definitions

**Item 6a**: Describe the study population, including any restrictions.

Restrictions on time period, age group, geographic region, or other strata [40–42] should be identified and justified to enable generalizability assessment [43].

**Item 6b**: Describe the nature and meaning of key variables.

Variables should be characterized as continuous, binary, or categorical. The handling of missing values (e.g., unspecified sex) should be detailed. For instance, criteria for classifying events as serious (death, hospitalization, life-threatening, disability) should be made explicit.

**Item 6c**: Specify and justify any grouping of drugs or events—including whether active ingredients, trade names, or salts were considered, and the assigned drug role.

Groupings should be referenced to existing taxonomies (MedDRA or ATC), standardized MedDRA queries (SMQs), previous literature, knowledge-engineering approaches, or detailed expert opinion with clinical rationale [43,46,47]. The role assignment for drugs (primary suspect, secondary/concomitant, interacting) should be specified.

**Item 6d**: Describe any additional data sources and how they interface with ICSRs.

Signal refinement and prioritization frequently require complementary data, including clinical trials, literature reviews, regulatory documents, labeled-ADR datasets [48], pharmacodynamic or pharmacokinetic evidence [49], and healthcare or claims databases [50]. Each external source and its linkage to the disproportionality results should be described.

### Item 7 — Statistical Methods

**Item 7a**: Present any descriptive analysis, including variables examined, statistical tests, and significance thresholds.

Descriptive analysis can reveal confounders, effect modifiers, and geographical patterns that reflect differences in pharmacovigilance systems, local regulatory warnings, and population characteristics.

**Item 7b**: Describe the disproportionality measure(s) selected, including thresholds for SDR identification, and explain the choice.

Common two-dimensional measures include the reporting odds ratio (ROR) [53], proportional reporting ratio (PRR) [54], information component (IC) [55], and the Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean [6,51,56,57]. For drug-drug interactions (three-dimensional analyses), Ω and the interaction signal score (INTSS) are used [58,59]. Authors should state the dimensionality of the measure, whether the analysis unit is ICSRs or drug-event pairs (more than one pair per ICSR), the comparator group (e.g., non-cases) [60], and any ICSR-count and statistical thresholds used for defining an SDR.

**Item 7c**: Clearly describe any sensitivity analysis and any tool to control confounding—including restriction, subgroup, stratification, adjustment, or interaction analyses.

Sensitivity and secondary analyses probe the robustness of primary findings to methodological assumptions and seek to control for confounding or effect modification to the extent feasible with ICSR data [3,61]. The guidelines refer readers to existing reviews for a full treatment of ICSR database biases [1,3,62,63].

**Item 7d**: Specify variables and methods used for case-by-case analysis, including causality assessment algorithms if performed.

Case-level synthesis is a central component of signal validation [64–67]. Variables to be examined include suspected drug role, concomitant medications, alternative causes, underlying disease, time to onset, dechallenge and rechallenge outcomes, dose, route, sex, age, and other events. Any causality assessment tool (e.g., WHO-UMC system) should be named.

**Item 7e**: Specify any statistical methods used for other data sources.

Because disproportionality analysis does not approximate risk estimates [68,69], any correlation between disproportionality results and external data (e.g., pharmacological mechanisms) should be acknowledged as exploratory [70,71].

### Item 8 — Description of Reports

**Item 8a**: Specify the number of ICSRs included at each stage, including reasons for exclusion.

The report should track ICSR counts through each study phase to enable sample-size evaluation and reproducibility. Exclusions should be attributed to identifiable reasons (duplicates, incomplete reports, exclusion criteria).

A flow diagram is recommended [72].

**Item 8b**: Provide key demographic and clinical characteristics of cases, with comparison to an appropriate reference group where possible.

Descriptive results help readers understand the study population and potential confounders such as age, sex, comorbidities, or concomitant drugs [42]. The appropriate reference group depends on the research question—for example, the entire database versus reports containing the same medication. Tabular presentation is encouraged.

### Item 9 — Results of Disproportionality Analyses

Present all results, including point estimates, confidence intervals, and sensitivity-analysis results.

Complete reporting allows readers to derive independent interpretations. Contingency-table figures and expected ICSR counts should be provided, at minimum in supplementary material.

### Item 10 — Results of Case-by-Case Analysis

Present the case-by-case analysis of key variables and the causality assessment.

The synthesis of ICSR-level features—including drug role, concomitant medications, alternative causes, underlying disease, time to onset, dechallenge/rechallenge outcomes, dose, route, sex, age, and co-reported events—enables evaluation of SDR validity. Missing values should be quantified. Anonymization may be necessary for rare diseases or drugs to prevent patient re-identification. A tabular listing of all assessed ICSRs and variables is recommended.

### Item 11 — Key Results

Discuss key results with reference to study objectives and contextualize them within the existing literature and other consulted sources. Clearly distinguish expected reactions from emerging safety signals.

Authors should integrate ICSR characteristics, disproportionality results, external evidence, and pharmacological plausibility to assess signal validity. Stakeholders must recognize that an SDR alone does not prove causation or permit incidence calculation or risk comparison between drugs [12,25,74,75]. Conversely, a lack of statistically significant disproportionality should not be interpreted as evidence of safety, nor an inverse signal as a protective effect [76]. Aggregated causality assessment should reference Bradford Hill guidelines [77–80].

The discussion should address: key findings, distinguishing expected reactions from novel signals; consistency or conflict with prior evidence; regulatory context, prescribing trends, and warnings; pharmacological plausibility (mechanism of action, pharmacokinetics); and negative findings contextualized through positive and negative control events.

### Item 12 — External Validity

**Item 12a**: Discuss the external validity of the results to the general population.

ICSR databases are typically more representative of real-world use than clinical trials, encompassing comorbidities, misuse, and comedication. However, if cases share peculiar features—for example, overdose or intentional misuse—identified safety concerns may not translate to routine clinical settings. Generalizability should be assessed with reference to setting, catchment area, disease prevalence, drug utilization, population characteristics, and unusual reporting patterns (e.g., litigation or solicited reports). Differences among countries in medication access, diagnostic procedures, regulatory warnings, and resulting reporting rates should be considered [81,82].

**Item 12b**: Discuss the potential relevance of results in clinical practice.

Risk-minimization proposals should integrate limitation-aware interpretation of disproportionality findings with evidence from all available sources. Recommendations may include label updates, additional monitoring, or use restrictions in specific populations, but providing clinical recommendations based on disproportionality analysis alone is discouraged.

**Item 12c**: Propose further study designs, if applicable.

When a safety signal is identified, specific confirmatory study designs or additional data sources (e.g., healthcare databases for hypothesis testing) should be proposed.

### Item 13 — Limitations

Present general limitations of ICSR databases and specific limitations of the implemented strategy. Make it clear that disproportionality analyses alone cannot prove causation or measure incidence, and address confounding and reporting bias and the efforts to mitigate them.

Disproportionality analysis is one step toward signal identification but cannot by itself establish causality or incidence due to the absence of patient-level exposure information [3,74], reporting biases [3,82], and confounding biases. The discussion should describe efforts to control for these factors through statistical methods or study design and acknowledge them as alternative explanations when residual uncertainty remains. Database adequacy and the completeness, coding accuracy, and consistency of key variables should be evaluated against study objectives.

### Item 14 — Declarations

**Item 14a**: Provide source of funding or sponsorship and the role of funders or sponsors.

Both financial (e.g., salary) and non-financial support (e.g., analytical services, access to commercial datasets) should be disclosed, with grant identifiers. Any involvement of funders in defining the question, collecting or analyzing data, interpreting results, or approving the final report should be explicitly stated or negated.

**Item 14b**: Clearly identify potential commercial and intellectual conflicts of interest—including links to investigated drugs or events, financial compensation, legal actions, or software ownership.

Relationships or activities that readers could consider pertinent should be disclosed. Management procedures for competing interests, where applicable, should be described.

**Item 14c**: Declare any institutional approval needed or granted—including Ethics Committee, Institutional Review Board, regulatory agency, or data-access committee—with the approving body's name and reference number.

**Item 14d**: Include statements on data availability, code availability (with statistical software version), and protocol registration.

Data and code should be shared in readily reusable formats (e.g., CSV), and repositories should provide persistent identifiers (DOI or URL). If legal or licensing restrictions prevent sharing, this limitation should be explicitly declared. The protocol should be cited with a URL or DOI, and the software name and version used for analyses should be recorded.

### Abstract Reporting (Additional Four Items)

The paper also specifies four items for the abstract: report key information on main objectives, methods, results, and implications. Abstracts should present results for all primary outcomes regardless of statistical significance, magnitude, or direction. Index terms should accurately describe the question (population, drug, event). Because abstracts are the most widely read and accessible portion of a paper, and because spin in disproportionality analysis abstracts is common—manifesting as overstated causal language, insufficient bias discussion, or over-extrapolation to clinical recommendations [12,20,25,74,75,84]—careful presentation of limitations in the abstract is particularly emphasized.

---

## Discussion

The READUS-PV guidelines represent the first consensus-based, internationally developed reporting standard specifically designed for disproportionality analyses using ICSR databases. By addressing 14 key elements across all sections of a scientific manuscript, they aim to equip authors with a structured framework for transparent reporting, enable editors and peer reviewers to evaluate completeness, and help readers interpret results with appropriate caution.

The need for such guidance is underscored by concurrent meta-epidemiological evidence. The nearly 75% spin prevalence documented by Mouffak and colleagues [12] and the finding by Khouri and colleagues that transparency and completeness of reporting are systematically lacking [11] indicate that the growth in publication volume has not been matched by improvements in methodological rigor or interpretive restraint. The rise from approximately 40 to 180 PubMed-indexed disproportionality analyses per year [9], in the absence of standardized reporting, risks both research waste and public health misdirection.

Several structural features of the READUS-PV framework merit emphasis. First, the guidelines insist on distinguishing expected reactions from novel safety signals in the discussion section, which addresses a recurring failure to contextualize disproportionality findings within existing evidence. Second, they mandate the reporting of negative results alongside positive and negative control events to establish assay sensitivity and specificity—a practice not yet standard in the field. Third, the requirement to disclose all data-preprocessing choices (extraction date, deduplication strategy, handling of missing data, variable derivation) targets a known source of irreproducibility. Fourth, by requiring explicit case-by-case synthesis and causality assessment, the guidelines seek to prevent overinterpretation of statistical signals detached from clinical plausibility.

The limitations of this work are primarily those inherent to any reporting guideline: adoption depends on the willingness of authors, journals, and reviewers to implement it, and the ultimate impact on evidence quality cannot be assessed until the guidelines have been in use for a sufficient period. The development of the checklist, detailed in the companion statement paper, was itself a consensus process subject to the composition and perspectives of the panel. Additionally, as the authors acknowledge, this paper is an explanation and elaboration document; the checklist's utility for specific sub-designs (e.g., drug-drug interaction analyses using Ω or INTSS measures, event-event co-occurrence analyses, or hybrid designs combining disproportionality with meta-analysis) is addressed in part by cross-references to other reporting checklists (Table 3 of the companion paper), but domain-specific refinements may be warranted in future iterations.

The authors conclude that widespread adoption and editorial endorsement of the READUS-PV guidelines will improve the transparency, completeness, and accuracy of disproportionality analysis reporting, leading to more robust evidence-based pharmacovigilance decision making and ultimately better patient care.
