# The REporting of A Disproportionality Analysis for DrUg Safety Signal Detection Using Individual Case Safety Reports in PharmacoVigilance (READUS-PV): Explanation and Elaboration

## Structured Scientific Account

- **Authors**: Fusaroli M, Salvo F, Begaud B, AlShammari TM, Bate A, Battini V, Brueckner A, Candore G, Carnovale C, Crisafulli S, Cutroneo PM, Dolladille C, Drici MD, Faillie JL, Goldman A, Hauben M, Herdeiro MT, Mahaux O, Manlik K, Montastruc F, Noguchi Y, Norén GN, Noseda R, Onakpoya IJ, Pariente A, Poluzzi E, Salem M, Sartori D, Trinh NTH, Tuccori M, van Hunsel F, van Puijenbroek E, Raschi E, Khouri C
- **Source**: *Drug Safety*, 2024 June
- **DOI**: [10.1007/s40264-024-01423-7](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40264-024-01423-7)
- **PMCID**: [PMC11116264](https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC11116264)
- **PMID**: [38713347](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38713347/)
- **Companion Statement Paper**: DOI [10.1007/s40264-024-01421-9](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40264-024-01421-9)
- **Protocol**: [https://readus-statement.org/](https://readus-statement.org/)
- **Reference Count**: 84
- **Retrieved from Europe PMC**: 2026-07-18

---

## Abstract

Disproportionality analyses of individual case safety report (ICSR) databases are a cornerstone of pharmacovigilance signal detection, yet their reporting has been hampered by inconsistency, incompleteness, and frequent interpretive distortion. In response, the international READUS-PV collaboration developed a set of 14 reporting recommendations across all manuscript sections (title through declarations), plus four additional items for abstracts. This explanation and elaboration paper provides the detailed justification for each retained item, alongside bullet-pointed implementation guidance. The guidelines are organized to span the title, introduction (background and objectives), methods (study design, database description, variable definitions, and statistical methods), results (report selection, disproportionality estimates, and case-by-case synthesis), discussion (key results, external validity, and limitations), and declarations (funding, conflicts of interest, institutional approvals, and data/code availability). Adoption of READUS-PV is intended to improve transparency, completeness, and accuracy in the reporting of disproportionality analyses and thereby support evidence-based pharmacovigilance decision making.

---

## Introduction

ICSR databases aggregate suspected adverse drug reaction reports from healthcare professionals and patients. Disproportionality analyses mine these databases to identify associations between drugs and adverse events that deviate from background reporting patterns; when combined with clinical review, they can reveal emerging safety concerns—particularly those unlikely to surface in premarketing clinical trials [2–7].

However, the volume of published disproportionality analyses has grown sharply. PubMed-indexed studies in this category climbed from approximately 40 in 2017 to roughly 180 in 2021 [9], a figure likely underestimated because of unsystematic terminology in reporting [8]. This increase risks overwhelming decision makers with noise and may also directly influence patients and clinical practice [10]. Critically, a meta-epidemiological investigation found that nearly 75% of published disproportionality analyses exhibit spin—inadequate reporting, overstated causal claims, or omission of biases that could explain observed associations [11,12]. Such distortions impede utilization and contribute to research waste [13–15].

To address these deficits, an international team developed the READUS-PV guidelines—the REporting of A Disproportionality analysis for drUg Safety signal detection using individual case safety reports in PharmacoVigilance [16]. The 14-item core checklist (plus four abstract items) was designed to assist authors in preparing transparent and reproducible articles, enable self-assessment and replication, promote proper interpretation of findings with their limitations, and aid reviewers and editors in evaluating submissions.

The READUS-PV output is published as two papers: a development and statement paper that describes the consensus process [17], and the present explanation and elaboration paper that substantiates each retained item with rationale and practical bullet points. The structure follows the EQUATOR Network model for reporting guideline documents [18].

---

## Methods (Guideline Development Summary)

The present paper is an explanation and elaboration document; the full development methodology is reported in the companion statement paper (DOI 10.1007/s40264-024-01421-9) [17]. In brief, the authors constituted an international panel of pharmacovigilance experts who followed a consensus-based approach to identify, refine, and select the final set of reporting recommendations. The protocol was preregistered on the EQUATOR registry and made available at [https://readus-statement.org/](https://readus-statement.org/).

The current explanation paper organizes the 14 retained items into the following domains: title; introduction (background and objectives); methods (study design, data description and preprocessing, variable definitions, and statistical methods); results (description of reports, disproportionality results, and case-by-case analysis results); discussion (key results, external validity, and limitations); and declarations. Each item is presented with (a) an explanation of the rationale for its inclusion and (b) essential bullet points that operationalize the recommendation. Additional sub-items are proposed where supplementary detail may enhance completeness or usability.

The companion paper's Table 3 also cross-references other published checklists for situations where the study design extends beyond a pure disproportionality analysis.

The study received a certification from the Research Ethics Committee of the University Hospital of Bordeaux that formal ethics submission was not required under French regulation. Funding was provided by Alma Mater Studiorum – Università di Bologna via the CRUI-CARE open-access agreement. Several co-authors disclosed employment relationships with pharmaceutical companies (Bayer AG, GSK, Pfizer) and declared stock ownership; the remaining authors declared no competing interests related to this work.

---

## Results: The 14 READUS-PV Reporting Items

### Item 1 — Title Information

**Item 1a**: The study should be identified as a "disproportionality analysis" in the title, and the type of data and database name should be specified.

Including the term "disproportionality analysis" facilitates database indexing, retrieval for systematic reviews, and appropriate reader context-setting. Non-specific labels (e.g., "data mining," "real-world study," "cross-sectional study," or "retrospective study") are discouraged because they obscure the study design and risk misinterpretation. The title should also name the data source (e.g., "ICSRs," or "social media" if applicable) and the specific database (e.g., FDA Adverse Event Reporting System [FAERS], EudraVigilance, VigiBase).

Additional recommendations: when other quantitative methods are used concurrently (e.g., a pharmacovigilance-pharmacodynamic analysis, a systematic review), this should be noted in the title. For hybrid designs where "disproportionality analysis" alone would be reductive, the term should appear at minimum among the keywords.

**Item 1b**: Report the name of adverse event(s) and/or drug(s) under study, when applicable.

The title should communicate the substantive focus—whether a specific drug-event combination, the overall safety profile of a drug (or a subgroup such as pediatric or pregnant populations), the iatrogenic determinants of a disease, or a methodological advancement.

### Item 2 — Background

**Item 2a**: Describe the drug(s) and their utilization, the nature and frequency of the adverse event(s), and the existing knowledge on the drug-event combination.

The introduction should summarize relevant drug features (international nonproprietary name, therapeutic class, mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, indications, and target populations) and adverse-event features (nature, clinical manifestations, severity, seriousness, and impact on quality of life). The specific knowledge gap should be justified by reference to prior evidence—previous disproportionality signals (e.g., elevated transaminases when liver failure is the focus), regulatory documents such as Summaries of Product Characteristics, and limitations of existing studies.

Additional information that may be considered includes brand names, formulations, administration routes, posology, dosing regimens, expected patient exposure, average duration of exposure, and background event rates, as these affect the number of reports received [21,22]. Approval dates and regulatory warnings may also be relevant [23,24].

**Item 2b**: Specify the rationale for performing the analysis—e.g., part of routine pharmacovigilance, investigation of an overall safety profile, or assessment of a prespecified hypothesis.

Disproportionality analyses typically originate from three contexts [25–27]: (1) agnostic or untargeted routine pharmacovigilance activities without a prespecified hypothesis; (2) investigation of the overall safety profile of a specific drug (e.g., under conditional accelerated approval or a risk management plan [28]); or (3) assessment of a prespecified evidence-based hypothesis grounded in pharmacological plausibility, recent case reports or series, or imbalances observed in clinical trials.

**Item 2c**: Explain why ICSR databases and disproportionality analysis are suitable for addressing the knowledge gap.

Authors should justify the appropriateness of spontaneous reporting data for the research question [29]. In particular, publication of a new disproportionality analysis should be preceded by careful consideration of existing pharmacoepidemiological or ICSR-based studies to avoid redundancy [25]. When substantial overlap exists with earlier work—for example, signals of disproportionate reporting (SDRs) from VigiBase versus FAERS [30]—replication studies must explicitly articulate their incremental contribution, such as a novel case-by-case analysis or adjustment for previously unrecognized biases.

### Item 3 — Objectives

State specific objectives, identifying the adverse event(s), the drug(s), the reference group, and any prespecified hypothesis.

An explicit and concise statement of aims—potentially framed using the PICO (population, intervention, comparator, outcome) or PEO (population, exposure, outcome) format [31,32]—should logically follow from the knowledge gap. Both primary and secondary objectives should be listed. Authors should also clarify when the analysis investigates relationships beyond simple drug-event associations, such as event-event co-occurrence [33], drug-indication-event relationships, or drug-drug interactions [34].

### Item 4 — Study Design

**Item 4a**: Identify the study as a "disproportionality analysis" and specify the data type (e.g., ICSRs).

Consistent terminology reduces ambiguity and aids appraisal. Standardized designation should be carried from title to methods.

**Item 4b**: Provide an outline of the entire study design, including primary and sensitivity analyses, and other components such as case-by-case analysis or literature review.

The design should be presented in a structured manner with justification for each operational choice. The primary analysis should be introduced with explicit reference to study objectives. Sensitivity and secondary analyses should be framed as efforts to address confounding, check assumptions, or investigate effect modifiers or subgroups. The presence or absence of a case-by-case causality assessment and/or systematic literature review should be stated.

For complex hybrid designs, a flow diagram is recommended. Authors may also consult the checklist cross-references provided in the companion statement paper (Table 3).

### Item 5 — Data Description, Access, and Preprocessing

**Item 5a**: Specify the database name, custodian, coverage, number of drugs, and the thesauri or ontologies used for coding drugs and events.

Database content directly determines the denominator of disproportionality calculations and influences results through reporting rates, drug utilization patterns, background event rates, and masking bias. The report should identify: the database(s) by name; the custodian entity; temporal and geographical coverage; the types of medicinal products captured (or the number and class of drugs, for industry databases); the coding systems—commonly the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) for events and Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classification for drugs [35,36]—including the version used; and the total number of reports in the database.

Additional considerations include justification for database choice, information on data collection and potential selection bias, and any quality-assurance measures applied.

**Item 5b**: Specify extraction dates and describe and justify all data-preprocessing choices, including transformations and exclusions.

Preprocessing decisions can alter the results and their interpretation [37,38]. Authors should report: the extraction or download date and access mechanism (e.g., online portal, data-sharing agreement, dashboard, quarterly data release) with a URL if available; any required approvals; restrictions on data access; procedures for identifying and removing duplicates, handling missing or nullified data, managing incongruous or inconsistent values, dealing with follow-up information, and standardizing data elements (e.g., free-text drug names to active ingredients); any derived variables (e.g., dose, time-to-onset, comorbidity proxies) and the assumptions underlying them; and any data exclusions applied.

### Item 6 — Variable Definitions

**Item 6a**: Describe the study population, including any restrictions.

Restrictions on time period, age group, geographic region, or other strata [40–42] should be identified and justified to enable generalizability assessment [43].

**Item 6b**: Describe the nature and meaning of key variables.

Variables should be characterized as continuous, binary, or categorical. The handling of missing values (e.g., unspecified sex) should be detailed. For instance, criteria for classifying events as serious (death, hospitalization, life-threatening, disability) should be made explicit.

**Item 6c**: Specify and justify any grouping of drugs or events—including whether active ingredients, trade names, or salts were considered, and the assigned drug role.

Groupings should be referenced to existing taxonomies (MedDRA or ATC), standardized MedDRA queries (SMQs), previous literature, knowledge-engineering approaches, or detailed expert opinion with clinical rationale [43,46,47]. The role assignment for drugs (primary suspect, secondary/concomitant, interacting) should be specified.

**Item 6d**: Describe any additional data sources and how they interface with ICSRs.

Signal refinement and prioritization frequently require complementary data, including clinical trials, literature reviews, regulatory documents, labeled-ADR datasets [48], pharmacodynamic or pharmacokinetic evidence [49], and healthcare or claims databases [50]. Each external source and its linkage to the disproportionality results should be described.

### Item 7 — Statistical Methods

**Item 7a**: Present any descriptive analysis, including variables examined, statistical tests, and significance thresholds.

Descriptive analysis can reveal confounders, effect modifiers, and geographical patterns that reflect differences in pharmacovigilance systems, local regulatory warnings, and population characteristics.

**Item 7b**: Describe the disproportionality measure(s) selected, including thresholds for SDR identification, and explain the choice.

Common two-dimensional measures include the reporting odds ratio (ROR) [53], proportional reporting ratio (PRR) [54], information component (IC) [55], and the Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean [6,51,56,57]. For drug-drug interactions (three-dimensional analyses), Ω and the interaction signal score (INTSS) are used [58,59]. Authors should state the dimensionality of the measure, whether the analysis unit is ICSRs or drug-event pairs (more than one pair per ICSR), the comparator group (e.g., non-cases) [60], and any ICSR-count and statistical thresholds used for defining an SDR.

**Item 7c**: Clearly describe any sensitivity analysis and any tool to control confounding—including restriction, subgroup, stratification, adjustment, or interaction analyses.

Sensitivity and secondary analyses probe the robustness of primary findings to methodological assumptions and seek to control for confounding or effect modification to the extent feasible with ICSR data [3,61]. The guidelines refer readers to existing reviews for a full treatment of ICSR database biases [1,3,62,63].

**Item 7d**: Specify variables and methods used for case-by-case analysis, including causality assessment algorithms if performed.

Case-level synthesis is a central component of signal validation [64–67]. Variables to be examined include suspected drug role, concomitant medications, alternative causes, underlying disease, time to onset, dechallenge and rechallenge outcomes, dose, route, sex, age, and other events. Any causality assessment tool (e.g., WHO-UMC system) should be named.

**Item 7e**: Specify any statistical methods used for other data sources.

Because disproportionality analysis does not approximate risk estimates [68,69], any correlation between disproportionality results and external data (e.g., pharmacological mechanisms) should be acknowledged as exploratory [70,71].

### Item 8 — Description of Reports

**Item 8a**: Specify the number of ICSRs included at each stage, including reasons for exclusion.

The report should track ICSR counts through each study phase to enable sample-size evaluation and reproducibility. Exclusions should be attributed to identifiable reasons (duplicates, incomplete reports, exclusion criteria).

A flow diagram is recommended [72].

**Item 8b**: Provide key demographic and clinical characteristics of cases, with comparison to an appropriate reference group where possible.

Descriptive results help readers understand the study population and potential confounders such as age, sex, comorbidities, or concomitant drugs [42]. The appropriate reference group depends on the research question—for example, the entire database versus reports containing the same medication. Tabular presentation is encouraged.

### Item 9 — Results of Disproportionality Analyses

Present all results, including point estimates, confidence intervals, and sensitivity-analysis results.

Complete reporting allows readers to derive independent interpretations. Contingency-table figures and expected ICSR counts should be provided, at minimum in supplementary material.

### Item 10 — Results of Case-by-Case Analysis

Present the case-by-case analysis of key variables and the causality assessment.

The synthesis of ICSR-level features—including drug role, concomitant medications, alternative causes, underlying disease, time to onset, dechallenge/rechallenge outcomes, dose, route, sex, age, and co-reported events—enables evaluation of SDR validity. Missing values should be quantified. Anonymization may be necessary for rare diseases or drugs to prevent patient re-identification. A tabular listing of all assessed ICSRs and variables is recommended.

### Item 11 — Key Results

Discuss key results with reference to study objectives and contextualize them within the existing literature and other consulted sources. Clearly distinguish expected reactions from emerging safety signals.

Authors should integrate ICSR characteristics, disproportionality results, external evidence, and pharmacological plausibility to assess signal validity. Stakeholders must recognize that an SDR alone does not prove causation or permit incidence calculation or risk comparison between drugs [12,25,74,75]. Conversely, a lack of statistically significant disproportionality should not be interpreted as evidence of safety, nor an inverse signal as a protective effect [76]. Aggregated causality assessment should reference Bradford Hill guidelines [77–80].

The discussion should address: key findings, distinguishing expected reactions from novel signals; consistency or conflict with prior evidence; regulatory context, prescribing trends, and warnings; pharmacological plausibility (mechanism of action, pharmacokinetics); and negative findings contextualized through positive and negative control events.

### Item 12 — External Validity

**Item 12a**: Discuss the external validity of the results to the general population.

ICSR databases are typically more representative of real-world use than clinical trials, encompassing comorbidities, misuse, and comedication. However, if cases share peculiar features—for example, overdose or intentional misuse—identified safety concerns may not translate to routine clinical settings. Generalizability should be assessed with reference to setting, catchment area, disease prevalence, drug utilization, population characteristics, and unusual reporting patterns (e.g., litigation or solicited reports). Differences among countries in medication access, diagnostic procedures, regulatory warnings, and resulting reporting rates should be considered [81,82].

**Item 12b**: Discuss the potential relevance of results in clinical practice.

Risk-minimization proposals should integrate limitation-aware interpretation of disproportionality findings with evidence from all available sources. Recommendations may include label updates, additional monitoring, or use restrictions in specific populations, but providing clinical recommendations based on disproportionality analysis alone is discouraged.

**Item 12c**: Propose further study designs, if applicable.

When a safety signal is identified, specific confirmatory study designs or additional data sources (e.g., healthcare databases for hypothesis testing) should be proposed.

### Item 13 — Limitations

Present general limitations of ICSR databases and specific limitations of the implemented strategy. Make it clear that disproportionality analyses alone cannot prove causation or measure incidence, and address confounding and reporting bias and the efforts to mitigate them.

Disproportionality analysis is one step toward signal identification but cannot by itself establish causality or incidence due to the absence of patient-level exposure information [3,74], reporting biases [3,82], and confounding biases. The discussion should describe efforts to control for these factors through statistical methods or study design and acknowledge them as alternative explanations when residual uncertainty remains. Database adequacy and the completeness, coding accuracy, and consistency of key variables should be evaluated against study objectives.

### Item 14 — Declarations

**Item 14a**: Provide source of funding or sponsorship and the role of funders or sponsors.

Both financial (e.g., salary) and non-financial support (e.g., analytical services, access to commercial datasets) should be disclosed, with grant identifiers. Any involvement of funders in defining the question, collecting or analyzing data, interpreting results, or approving the final report should be explicitly stated or negated.

**Item 14b**: Clearly identify potential commercial and intellectual conflicts of interest—including links to investigated drugs or events, financial compensation, legal actions, or software ownership.

Relationships or activities that readers could consider pertinent should be disclosed. Management procedures for competing interests, where applicable, should be described.

**Item 14c**: Declare any institutional approval needed or granted—including Ethics Committee, Institutional Review Board, regulatory agency, or data-access committee—with the approving body's name and reference number.

**Item 14d**: Include statements on data availability, code availability (with statistical software version), and protocol registration.

Data and code should be shared in readily reusable formats (e.g., CSV), and repositories should provide persistent identifiers (DOI or URL). If legal or licensing restrictions prevent sharing, this limitation should be explicitly declared. The protocol should be cited with a URL or DOI, and the software name and version used for analyses should be recorded.

### Abstract Reporting (Additional Four Items)

The paper also specifies four items for the abstract: report key information on main objectives, methods, results, and implications. Abstracts should present results for all primary outcomes regardless of statistical significance, magnitude, or direction. Index terms should accurately describe the question (population, drug, event). Because abstracts are the most widely read and accessible portion of a paper, and because spin in disproportionality analysis abstracts is common—manifesting as overstated causal language, insufficient bias discussion, or over-extrapolation to clinical recommendations [12,20,25,74,75,84]—careful presentation of limitations in the abstract is particularly emphasized.

---

## Discussion

The READUS-PV guidelines represent the first consensus-based, internationally developed reporting standard specifically designed for disproportionality analyses using ICSR databases. By addressing 14 key elements across all sections of a scientific manuscript, they aim to equip authors with a structured framework for transparent reporting, enable editors and peer reviewers to evaluate completeness, and help readers interpret results with appropriate caution.

The need for such guidance is underscored by concurrent meta-epidemiological evidence. The nearly 75% spin prevalence documented by Mouffak and colleagues [12] and the finding by Khouri and colleagues that transparency and completeness of reporting are systematically lacking [11] indicate that the growth in publication volume has not been matched by improvements in methodological rigor or interpretive restraint. The rise from approximately 40 to 180 PubMed-indexed disproportionality analyses per year [9], in the absence of standardized reporting, risks both research waste and public health misdirection.

Several structural features of the READUS-PV framework merit emphasis. First, the guidelines insist on distinguishing expected reactions from novel safety signals in the discussion section, which addresses a recurring failure to contextualize disproportionality findings within existing evidence. Second, they mandate the reporting of negative results alongside positive and negative control events to establish assay sensitivity and specificity—a practice not yet standard in the field. Third, the requirement to disclose all data-preprocessing choices (extraction date, deduplication strategy, handling of missing data, variable derivation) targets a known source of irreproducibility. Fourth, by requiring explicit case-by-case synthesis and causality assessment, the guidelines seek to prevent overinterpretation of statistical signals detached from clinical plausibility.

The limitations of this work are primarily those inherent to any reporting guideline: adoption depends on the willingness of authors, journals, and reviewers to implement it, and the ultimate impact on evidence quality cannot be assessed until the guidelines have been in use for a sufficient period. The development of the checklist, detailed in the companion statement paper, was itself a consensus process subject to the composition and perspectives of the panel. Additionally, as the authors acknowledge, this paper is an explanation and elaboration document; the checklist's utility for specific sub-designs (e.g., drug-drug interaction analyses using Ω or INTSS measures, event-event co-occurrence analyses, or hybrid designs combining disproportionality with meta-analysis) is addressed in part by cross-references to other reporting checklists (Table 3 of the companion paper), but domain-specific refinements may be warranted in future iterations.

The authors conclude that widespread adoption and editorial endorsement of the READUS-PV guidelines will improve the transparency, completeness, and accuracy of disproportionality analysis reporting, leading to more robust evidence-based pharmacovigilance decision making and ultimately better patient care.
